# On Having Nothing in Particular to Say

There's a peculiar pressure in being asked to write about anything at all. It's harder than writing about something specific. Give me a topic—the migration patterns of Arctic terns, the history of the semicolon, why people stopped using fax machines—and I can move forward with purpose. But "whatever comes to mind" puts me in a room with no walls, and I have to build the walls myself before I can lean against them.

I keep thinking about the word "whatever" itself, actually. It's strange how a word can mean both "anything, I don't care which" and, in teenage vernacular, a kind of dismissive shrug—*whatever*—as if the multiplicity of options has curdled into indifference. Too much freedom and the mind sometimes collapses into a shrug. This is maybe why constraints help creativity rather than hurting it. A sonnet's fourteen lines aren't a cage so much as a trellis. The vine still has to grow, but it has something to climb.

So let me give myself a small constraint, invented on the spot: I'll let one thought lead to the next, the way you do in those half-awake minutes before actually getting out of bed, when your brain free-associates without much editorial control. Call it controlled drift.

Here's where it goes: bed, mornings, the specific quality of light through a window in early autumn—not summer's assault of brightness, not winter's stinginess, but something more diplomatic, a light that seems to negotiate with the room rather than conquer it. I associate that light with a kind of mental clarity that I don't get any other time of day. There's research on this, I think—something about cortisol and circadian rhythms—but I'm more interested in the phenomenology than the biochemistry. The feeling of a mind that hasn't yet accumulated the day's debris. No emails read, no small humiliations or minor triumphs yet metabolized, no decisions made that you'll second-guess by 3 p.m.

This is the closest thing to a blank page that a human gets, and yet most of us spend it scrolling.

I don't say that to moralize—I'm not interested in being a scold about phones, that's a tired genre at this point, everyone already knows and nobody changes—but I am interested in the strangeness of having unprecedented access to the thoughts of millions of strangers at the exact moment when your own thoughts are most unformed and impressionable. It's like inviting a crowd into a room before you've had coffee. You're not at your most discerning. Whatever they're carrying, you end up carrying too, at least for a few minutes.

Which brings me, by the drift-logic I promised, to the idea of carrying things that aren't yours. Moods are contagious in a way that's almost embarrassing when you notice it happening. You can walk into a room cheerful and walk out flat, and if you trace it back, it's because someone else was flat first and you, porous creature that you are, picked it up like a cold. We don't have very good language for this kind of transmission. We talk about "vibes," which is doing a lot of conceptual work for such a flimsy word. The Victorians might have called it "atmosphere" and meant something almost meteorological by it—a pressure system moving through a room, dropping or raising the emotional barometer of everyone inside.

I wonder if writing is partly an attempt to stabilize this. To take the atmospheric and pin it down into something with edges. A feeling, left to itself, will drift and mutate and eventually dissipate into something you can no longer name; but a sentence about the feeling has a shape, and shapes are easier to hold. This might be why people keep journals even when no one will ever read them. Not communication, exactly—more like taxidermy for moods. You're not trying to share the feeling. You're trying to stop it from disappearing entirely.

Of course, the taxidermied version is never quite the living thing. Anyone who's tried to revisit an old journal knows this. You read your own words from three years ago and think, *did I feel that? Really?* The sentence is intact, but the heat behind it is gone. This used to bother me more than it does now. I've come around to thinking that's simply what time does to feeling, and there's no betrayal in it, no failure of the writing. The words were never supposed to be a freezer. They were more like a photograph of a wave at the beach. The wave is long gone by the time you're looking at the photo. That doesn't make the photo a lie.

I notice I've moved a long way from where I started—from "whatever" to mornings to phones to vibes to journals—and if I look back at the path I can see the logic of each step even though I couldn't have planned the route in advance. This is, I think, what's actually being requested when someone says "write whatever comes to mind." Not nothing. Not randomness. But a kind of trust in association, in the idea that one true thought, followed honestly, tends to lead to another. The thread isn't there before you start pulling it. It only becomes a thread because you keep pulling.

Maybe that's the whole answer to the original problem, the room with no walls. You don't need the walls ahead of time. You build them as you go, one sentence acting as the foundation for the next, until eventually you turn around and see that you've made an actual room, with a door, even though you walked in not knowing if there would be a floor.
